case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, consistent with Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b), a district court may admit a law-enforcement expert’s testimony that drug-trafficking organizations typically do not use unwitting couriers to import large drug shipments, given its practical effect on the jury’s determination of the defendant’s knowledge (mens rea).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b) (opinions on ultimate issue in criminal cases concerning a defendant’s mental state).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Diaz argues that the challenged expert testimony is effectively an opinion on the defendant’s knowledge—i.e., it tells the jury that most people in her position knew they were carrying drugs—so it functions as an impermissible mens rea shortcut that invades the jury’s role and violates Rule 704(b) by indirectly stating (or compelling) the conclusion that she knew about the drugs.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that Rule 704(b) bars only direct expert opinions about the particular defendant’s mental state (e.g., 'Diaz knew'), not generalized 'framework' or modus-operandi testimony about drug-trafficking practices; the expert testified about typical organizational behavior and left the ultimate inference about Diaz’s knowledge to the jury, so the district court acted within its discretion in admitting the testimony.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the hardest point: in a courier case, “traffickers typically do not use unwitting couriers” can feel like a mens rea shortcut and risks jurors treating a generalization as a substitute for individualized proof. But Rule 704(b) draws a textual and administrable line at expert opinions “about whether the defendant did or did not have” the requisite mental state, and—consistent with Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s focus on that boundary—this testimony, framed as general modus operandi rather than a case-specific conclusion about Diaz, does not cross it. Treating “practical effect” as the trigger would expand 704(b) beyond its terms and collapse it into a broad prejudice rule better handled through Rules 702 and 403, with limiting instructions and careful gatekeeping. Sandstrom’s mandatory-presumption concern remains materially different here, as Justice Thomas and Justice Alito note, because the jury is not directed to find knowledge nor is the burden shifted.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best objection: in a courier case, the statement that traffickers “typically do not use unwitting couriers” may operate as a de facto conclusion that this defendant knew. But under the enacted text of Rule 704(b), the prohibition turns on whether the expert offers an opinion “about whether the defendant did or did not have” the requisite mental state; as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch explain, generalized modus-operandi testimony is not, by its terms, about Diaz’s mental state, even if it strengthens an inference the jury may draw. Treating “practical effect” as the test would rewrite the statutory line Congress chose and collapse 704(b) into an atextual, categorical prejudice rule better handled through Rules 702/403 and limiting instructions. Sandstrom’s due-process concern with mandatory presumptions does not control because this testimony neither directed a finding of knowledge nor shifted the burden—it left the jury free to accept or reject the inference.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor (joined in part by Justice Jackson) makes the best practical point: in a courier case where knowledge is the only live issue, “traffickers typically don’t use unwitting couriers” can function as a powerful shortcut that risks substituting general probabilities for an individualized mens rea finding. But Rule 704(b) draws a textual boundary at an expert opinion about whether “the defendant did or did not have” the requisite mental state, and—as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize—generalized modus-operandi testimony about how organizations operate is not, by its terms, an opinion about Diaz’s actual knowledge. Sandstrom does not meaningfully move the needle because it concerns mandatory presumptions that relieve the prosecution of its burden, whereas this testimony supports only a permissive inference that remains subject to ordinary burden-of-proof instructions and adversarial testing. The proper way to deal with Sotomayor’s “shortcut” concern is through Rules 702 and 403 (and, where appropriate, limiting instructions), not by expanding 704(b) beyond its administrable text into a “functional equivalent” doctrine.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s textual point—that Rule 704(b) speaks in terms of an opinion “about whether the defendant” had the mental state—is the hardest for me, and I accept that courts must preserve an administrable line. But in this kind of courier case, the officer’s categorical claim that traffickers “typically do not use unwitting couriers” is so tightly keyed to the only contested element that it is, in substance, an opinion about Diaz’s knowledge, inviting the jury to treat a generalized probability as a substitute for individualized proof—precisely the end-run 704(b) was designed to block. Justice Kagan is right that Rule 403 often does work, yet relying on 403 and limiting instructions here understates the real-world evidentiary power of law-enforcement “profile” testimony to create a presumption-like inference, especially against a vulnerable defendant with little ability to rebut the expert’s asserted experience. Sandstrom may not control, as Justice Gorsuch notes, but its due-process warning about devices that effectively relieve the government of proving mens rea supports reading 704(b) to prevent experts from converting “general practice” into a functional mens rea conclusion in the defendant’s case.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s functional-equivalence argument has real force in a courier case where knowledge is the only live issue, because “typically not unwitting couriers” risks becoming a shortcut jurors treat as dispositive. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Rule 704(b) draws a textual boundary: it excludes an expert’s opinion about whether “the defendant” had the requisite mental state, and testimony framed as general trafficking practice—even if highly suggestive—remains about organizational modus operandi rather than Diaz’s mind. If we extend 704(b) to cover any testimony with strong practical effect on mens rea, we convert it into a broad prejudice screen better administered (and more textually anchored) through Rules 702/403 plus limiting instructions. Justice Jackson’s Sandstrom-inflected due-process concern underscores why trial judges should be vigilant under 403, but it does not justify rewriting 704(b) where the jury is not instructed to presume knowledge and remains free to reject the inference.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is the functional-risk: in a courier case, “traffickers typically don’t use unwitting couriers” can feel like a mens rea conclusion and may powerfully influence a jury. But Rule 704(b)’s text—stressed by Chief Justice Roberts—bars an expert opinion “about whether the defendant did or did not have” the mental state; testimony framed as general modus operandi is not, by its terms, about Diaz’s knowledge, and extending the Rule to cover “functional equivalents” would rewrite Congress’s line. Sandstrom does not undermine that textual boundary because it addresses mandatory presumptions that relieve the State’s burden, whereas this evidence at most supports a permissive inference still tested through adversarial process, Rule 702 reliability constraints, and Rule 403 balancing. I would therefore affirm on the narrow ground Roberts outlines: police case-specific mens rea opinions under 704(b), and address overreach in generalized framework testimony through 702/403 and limiting instructions rather than expanding 704(b) beyond its words.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s functional-equivalence point has real force in a courier case where knowledge is the only live issue, and I share the concern that the “unwitting couriers are not typically used” phrasing can be outcome-determinative in practice. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Rule 704(b) sets an administrable, text-based boundary—opinions about whether “the defendant did or did not have” the mental state—and this testimony, framed as general modus operandi, does not cross into a case-specific conclusion about Diaz’s mens rea. Justice Jackson’s Sandstrom-inflected fairness concern does not, in my view, supply a doctrinal basis to rewrite 704(b), because Sandstrom addressed mandatory presumptions that shift or dilute the burden, whereas here the inference remains permissive and is better policed through Rules 702/403 and limiting instructions. Expanding 704(b) to reach evidence based on its “practical effect” would destabilize settled evidentiary practice and effectively convert 704(b) into a broad prejudice rule untethered to the line Congress drew.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the most serious concern: in a courier case, “typically do not use unwitting couriers” can function as a de facto mens rea conclusion, inviting jurors to treat a generalization as proof of Diaz’s knowledge. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Rule 704(b) is triggered by an expert “opinion … about whether the defendant did or did not have” the mental state, and a textualist approach cannot convert powerful inferential evidence into a categorical bar untethered to what the opinion is about. The due-process analogy to Sandstrom is not persuasive here because, unlike a mandatory presumption, this testimony does not direct a finding or shift any burden; the remaining risk of overvaluation is better addressed through Rules 702 and 403 (and limiting instructions) rather than by expanding 704(b)’s scope. I therefore would affirm on the narrow ground Roberts identifies: permit generalized modus-operandi testimony while policing case-specific or unavoidable “Diaz knew” conclusions under 704(b) and prejudice under 403.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s textual point—that Rule 704(b) speaks of opinions about “the defendant,” and this was framed as general practice—is the strongest counterargument, and I take seriously the administrability concern Justice Kagan raises about collapsing 704(b) into 403. But in a case where knowledge is the only real contested element, the officer’s categorical “typically do not use unwitting couriers” testimony functions as an opinion about Diaz’s mental state in all but name, inviting jurors to substitute an expert’s probabilistic generalization for the individualized mens rea determination Rule 704(b) was designed to protect, as Justice Sotomayor explains. Sandstrom is not directly controlling, as Justice Gorsuch notes, yet its due-process warning about devices that effectively relieve the government of proving mens rea reinforces why we should read 704(b) with attention to practical consequences rather than formal labels. Rules 403/702 and limiting instructions are not an adequate backstop here because the specific vice is the expert’s end-run around the ultimate-issue bar, not merely “prejudice” in the ordinary sense.

John Roberts.reasoning: Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b) bars an expert from stating an opinion “about whether the defendant did or did not have a mental state or condition that constitutes an element of the crime charged,” but it does not categorically exclude modus-operandi testimony that merely supports an inference the jury may draw for itself. Consistent with the approach reflected in United States v. Morales, 108 F.3d 1031, 1038 (9th Cir. 1997) (en banc), the challenged testimony described typical drug-trafficking practices and did not directly opine that Diaz herself knew about the drugs, leaving the ultimate mens rea determination to the jury. While such testimony may carry substantial practical weight, that concern is addressed through Rule 403 balancing and limiting instructions rather than an expanded reading of 704(b) that would disrupt established evidentiary practice across circuits. A narrow affirmance on these grounds best respects the text of Rule 704(b), prevailing precedent, and institutional legitimacy, without endorsing any mandatory inference of knowledge forbidden by cases like Sandstrom v. Montana, 442 U.S. 510 (1979).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b) prohibits an expert from stating an “opinion or inference” that the defendant “did or did not have the mental state…constituting an element of the crime,” but it does not bar generalized modus-operandi testimony about how drug-trafficking organizations typically operate. The challenged testimony described common organizational practices (that large shipments are not usually entrusted to unwitting couriers) and did not opine that Diaz herself knew she carried drugs, leaving the ultimate mens rea determination to the jury consistent with the Rule’s text and its 1984 enactment aimed at preventing expert conclusions on the ultimate issue. Unlike the compelled-presumption problem in Sandstrom v. Montana, 442 U.S. 510 (1979), this evidence did not instruct the jury to presume knowledge; it merely provided a framework from which jurors could draw (or reject) an inference. Because the testimony falls outside Rule 704(b)’s precise textual prohibition, admitting it was consistent with the Rule and within the district court’s evidentiary discretion.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b) bars an expert from stating an opinion about whether the particular defendant did or did not have the requisite mental state, but it does not categorically forbid generalized modus-operandi testimony that provides the jury a framework for assessing evidence. Testimony that drug-trafficking organizations typically avoid using unwitting couriers for large shipments describes organizational practice and leaves the ultimate inference about Diaz’s knowledge to the jury, so it is not the “functional equivalent” of saying “Diaz knew,” even if it has practical force. The proper check on any undue prejudice is the ordinary application of Rules 702 and 403 and careful limiting instructions, not an overbroad reading of 704(b) that would hamstring law-enforcement experts in explaining how sophisticated trafficking schemes operate. Sandstrom v. Montana concerns mandatory presumptions that relieve the Government of proving mens rea beyond a reasonable doubt; this testimony creates no mandatory presumption and does not compel the jury to find knowledge.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b) bars expert testimony that, in substance, tells the jury what mental-state conclusion to reach, and an officer’s assertion that drug-trafficking organizations “typically do not use unwitting couriers” in large shipments functions as a practical mens rea shortcut in a case where knowledge is the central disputed issue. Even if phrased as general modus-operandi evidence, it invites the jury to treat the defendant’s claimed lack of knowledge as implausible because “people like her” usually know—effectively substituting an expert’s inference for the jury’s determination of Diaz’s knowledge, contrary to Rule 704(b)’s purpose and fairness constraints. Given the risk that such testimony creates an outcome-determinative presumption against the defendant’s innocence, courts should enforce Rule 704(b) more robustly rather than allowing formalistic wording to evade the Rule’s protection. This approach aligns with due-process concerns about evidentiary devices that operate like presumptions on an element of the offense, as cautioned in Sandstrom v. Montana, 442 U.S. 510 (1979).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Rule 704(b) by its text bars an expert from stating an opinion “about whether the defendant did or did not have a mental state … that constitutes an element,” and this testimony—framed as a general practice of drug-trafficking organizations rather than “Diaz knew”—does not directly opine on Diaz’s actual knowledge. Properly understood as modus-operandi or “framework” evidence, it can help the jury evaluate the plausibility of an unwitting-courier defense while leaving the ultimate mens rea determination to the jury, with residual protections coming from Rules 401 and 403 and limiting instructions. Although Diaz is right that such evidence can be powerfully suggestive, treating all generalized practice testimony as a functional 704(b) violation would extend the Rule beyond its textual boundary and risk undermining workable evidentiary lines in courier cases. Sandstrom v. Montana underscores the constitutional concern with compelled inferences about mens rea, but that problem is mitigated here because the testimony did not create a mandatory presumption and the jury remained free to accept or reject the inference.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Rule 704(b) by its text bars an expert from stating an “opinion about whether the defendant did or did not have a mental state” that constitutes an element, and the testimony here was framed as a generalized description of drug-trafficking organizations’ typical practices rather than an opinion that Diaz herself “knew.” That kind of modus-operandi “framework” evidence may be relevant and admissible so long as the expert does not cross the line into an explicit conclusion about the particular defendant’s mens rea; the ultimate inference remains for the jury, subject to Rules 401 and 403. While petitioner invokes concerns akin to Sandstrom v. Montana about effectively directing the jury on an element, this record describes permissive background testimony rather than a mandatory presumption or an expert’s direct statement of Diaz’s knowledge. On a textualist view, expanding 704(b) to cover testimony with merely a “practical effect” on the jury’s inference would go beyond the Rule’s expressed limit to opinions about “the defendant” and would risk turning many relevant expert explanations into categorical exclusions.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b) by its text bars expert opinions about whether “the defendant did or did not have” the requisite mental state, but it does not categorically exclude generalized modus-operandi testimony about how drug-trafficking organizations typically operate. Here, the officer’s testimony that traffickers generally do not use unwitting couriers speaks to common practices and provides context for the jury’s evaluation, without directly stating that Diaz herself knew about the drugs—leaving the ultimate mens rea inference to the jury and fitting within the prevailing circuit approach that draws a “fine but critical line” between general framework testimony and case-specific mental-state opinions. Practical workability and precedent counsel against expanding 704(b) to cover any testimony that may bear on knowledge indirectly, which would destabilize long-accepted uses of expert testimony in drug cases and shift evidentiary line-drawing away from trial-court discretion. Sandstrom v. Montana is not controlling because it concerns unconstitutional mandatory presumptions that relieve the State of proof, whereas the challenged testimony does not instruct the jury to presume knowledge and remains subject to adversarial testing and ordinary burden-of-proof instructions.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b) bars an expert from stating an opinion “about whether the defendant did or did not have a mental state or condition that constitutes an element of the crime charged.” By its text and ordinary operation, that prohibition targets direct testimony about this defendant’s mens rea (e.g., “Diaz knew”), not generalized modus-operandi testimony describing how drug-trafficking organizations typically structure large shipments. While such testimony may have substantial persuasive force on the knowledge inference, Rule 704(b) does not exclude evidence merely because it bears on an ultimate issue; other rules (especially Rules 702 and 403) perform that gatekeeping, and the district court did not violate 704(b) by admitting a general practice statement that left the ultimate inference to the jury. Sandstrom v. Montana addresses mandatory presumptions that relieve the State of proving mens rea beyond a reasonable doubt, but this expert testimony did not create a binding presumption or shift the burden; it remained for the jury to decide knowledge from all the evidence.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b) bars expert opinion testimony in a criminal case that, in practical effect, tells the jury whether the defendant had the requisite mens rea, and the law-enforcement expert’s assertion that drug-trafficking organizations “typically do not use unwitting couriers” functions as a near-direct inference that Diaz knew about the drugs. Even if framed as generalized modus-operandi evidence, the testimony risks becoming the “functional equivalent” of an opinion on Diaz’s knowledge, substituting an expert’s profile-based generalization for the jury’s individualized assessment and undermining procedural fairness in a context where liberty is at stake. That concern is heightened where, as here, the government’s proof of knowledge is largely circumstantial and the expert’s generalization can operate like an evidentiary shortcut akin to an improper presumption, contrary to the due process principles reflected in Sandstrom v. Montana. The district court therefore should have excluded (or tightly limited) this testimony under Rule 704(b) to prevent an end-run around the rule’s core protection for the jury’s role on mens rea.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, under Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b), a law-enforcement expert may testify that drug-trafficking organizations generally do not use unwitting couriers for large drug shipments—testimony that effectively implies the defendant knew about the drugs.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b) (limits expert testimony on a criminal defendant’s mental state as an element of the crime).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Diaz argues the district court improperly admitted expert testimony about how drug couriers typically operate because, in context, it functioned as an opinion on her mens rea (knowledge), the central disputed element. Although framed as general “drug-trafficking organization practices,” the testimony invited the jury to infer that because large shipments are usually entrusted only to knowing couriers, Diaz must have known she was transporting methamphetamine. Petitioner (supported by defense amici) contends this is exactly the kind of end-run around Rule 704(b) the Rule was designed to prevent, risks converting probabilistic generalizations into de facto proof of intent, and can operate like an impermissible presumption on mens rea (analogized to constitutional concerns reflected in cases like Sandstrom).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States contends the district court acted within its discretion in admitting the testimony because Rule 704(b) bars only direct expert opinions about the defendant’s mental state (e.g., “she knew”), not background or “framework” testimony describing common practices in drug trafficking. The government emphasizes the expert spoke in generalities about drug-trafficking organizations and couriers (how these crimes are typically carried out), leaving the ultimate inference about Diaz’s knowledge to the jury. Respondent and supporting evidence-professor amici also argue such framework evidence is common, useful to help jurors understand unfamiliar criminal methods, and that a broader reading of 704(b) would create significant line-drawing problems and destabilize admissibility of many kinds of expert context testimony in criminal trials.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan make the best case that “about whether” can reach functional equivalents and that a near-categorical statement like “traffickers don’t use unwitting couriers” risks becoming an end-run around Rule 704(b). But under a minimalist, text-and-precedent anchored approach, I remain persuaded—consistent with Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas—that 704(b) is best read to bar expert opinions on this defendant’s mental state, not general modus-operandi testimony from which the jury may (permissibly) infer knowledge; otherwise courts would be forced into unstable line-drawing that effectively narrows 704(a) far beyond Congress’s carveout. Justice Sotomayor’s Sandstrom concern identifies a real danger of undue weight, yet it is materially different from a mandatory presumption and is better handled through Rules 702 and 403 (and careful limiting instructions) than by expanding 704(b)’s reach beyond its administrable core. On this record—where the expert stayed in general terms and did not say Diaz knew—I would affirm on narrow grounds while warning district courts to police reliability and prejudice closely.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that “about whether” can capture functional equivalents and thus prevent an easy end-run around Rule 704(b). But under the Rule’s text as originally understood, an “opinion about whether the defendant did or did not have” the mental state targets testimony that directly addresses this defendant’s mental condition, not generalized modus-operandi propositions that merely supply circumstantial context from which the jury may draw its own inference. As Justice Gorsuch and the Chief Justice emphasize, a “functional equivalent” test would be atextual and indeterminate—forcing courts to guess how close is “too close”—and would, in practice, sweep broadly across routine expert background evidence in a way that effectively contracts Rule 704(a) beyond Congress’s narrow carveout. Justice Sotomayor’s Sandstrom-based concern underscores the need for vigilant trial-court policing, but that risk is better handled through Rules 702 and 403 (and limiting instructions) rather than rewriting 704(b)’s defendant-focused prohibition.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point—that “about whether” should reach functional equivalents to prevent artful evasion—has force as a policy matter, but it is not the best reading of Rule 704(b)’s narrow text, which targets opinions on whether this defendant had the requisite mental state, not generalized modus-operandi evidence from which jurors may draw their own inference. As the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, a functional-equivalent test would be administratively unstable and would in practice convert 704(b) into an indeterminate ban on common expert background testimony whenever knowledge is disputed, effectively contracting Rule 704(a) beyond Congress’s specific carveout. Justice Sotomayor’s Sandstrom analogy underscores a legitimate risk of undue persuasion, but Sandstrom concerned mandatory, burden-shifting legal presumptions; here the jury remains free to reject the inference, and the better tools to police overreach are Rules 702 and 403 (plus limiting instructions), not expanding 704(b) beyond its phrasing. Justice Thomas’s citation to DiDomenico and Morales reinforces that the historically workable line—excluding explicit mens rea opinions about the defendant—fits both text and practice and was not crossed on this record.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is administrability: a bright line limited to explicit opinions about this defendant’s mental state is easy to apply and leaves the rest to Rules 403/702 and instructions. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, the text bars expert opinions “about whether” the defendant had the mental state, and that naturally reaches testimony whose probative thrust in context is to answer the knowledge question by near-categorical generalization (“traffickers don’t use unwitting couriers”) when knowledge is the sole disputed element. Justice Thomas’s reliance on DiDomenico and Morales shows a narrower circuit gloss, but it also illustrates how easily Rule 704(b) can be evaded by swapping “Diaz knew” for “people like Diaz always know,” which undermines 704(b)’s allocation-of-decisionmaker function in a way 403/702 cannot reliably cure. Sandstrom is not controlling, yet the practical risk of jurors treating law-enforcement expertise as a shortcut to mens rea remains precisely why I would read “about whether” to cover functional equivalents in this narrow posture.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s administrability concern is the most serious point for the Respondent, and I agree with him and Justice Gorsuch that 704(b) cannot become an unmoored “close enough” test that chills legitimate background testimony. But Justice Barrett is right that the text—an opinion “about whether the defendant did or did not have” the mental state—does not naturally confine itself to defendant-naming sentences; it reaches testimony whose evident purpose in context is to answer the very “whether” question on mens rea by substituting a classwide near-categorical rule for the defendant-specific inference. Justice Thomas’s reliance on DiDomenico and Morales shows a longstanding circuit gloss, but as a matter of statutory coherence that practice reads “about whether” too narrowly and invites the drafting-game evasion our Rule should not encourage, especially where the generalization is keyed to the defendant’s posture and used to prove knowledge. I remain persuaded that Rules 702/403 are necessary backstops, yet they do not do the same work as 704(b)’s allocation-of-decisionmaker function, which is precisely to prevent expert authority from supplying (directly or effectively) the dispositive mens rea inference.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s best point is that “about whether” can capture functional equivalents and prevent artful evasion, but that reading departs from the ordinary sense of an opinion “about whether the defendant” had a mental state—i.e., a judgment directed at this defendant’s own mind rather than a general observation about typical trafficking practices. As the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas stress, a functional-equivalent test invites atextual line-drawing and would predictably swallow Rule 704(a) in cases where modus-operandi testimony is routinely offered for permissible purposes (context, methods, concealment), leaving courts to guess how “close” is too close. Justice Sotomayor’s Sandstrom concern is a serious prudential warning, yet Sandstrom addressed mandatory legal presumptions; the better textual fit is to keep 704(b) to direct mens rea opinions and rely on Rules 702 and 403 (and instructions) to police overbearing or unreliable generalizations. The circuit practice Justice Thomas cites (e.g., DiDomenico; Morales) does not control the meaning of the Rule, but it corroborates that an administrable, historically grounded line exists and can be applied without rewriting “about whether” into an unbounded proxy-for-guilt standard.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan make the strongest textual case that “about whether” can reach functional equivalents, and I appreciate the evasion concern (experts swapping “Diaz knew” for “couriers like Diaz always know”). But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch that anchoring Rule 704(b) to explicit opinions on this defendant’s mental state supplies an administrable, historically stable line consistent with how courts have long handled modus-operandi testimony, while a functional-equivalent test risks unpredictable, case-by-case line drawing that would chill ordinary background evidence and effectively narrow Rule 704(a) beyond Congress’s targeted carveout. Justice Sotomayor’s Sandstrom analogy highlights a real fairness risk, yet Sandstrom’s problem was a mandatory, burden-shifting presumption; here the inference remains permissive and is better policed through rigorous Rule 702 reliability review, Rule 403 prejudice balancing, and careful limiting instructions rather than expanding 704(b) beyond its clear core. On this record—generalized testimony without an express conclusion that Diaz knew—I would affirm, while emphasizing trial courts must scrutinize sweeping “unwitting courier” generalizations closely under 702/403 to protect the jury’s role.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s administrability concern is the Respondent’s strongest point, but it depends on reading “about whether the defendant did or did not have” as limited to an explicit, defendant-specific mens rea conclusion; that narrowing is hard to square with the ordinary public meaning of “about whether,” which naturally covers statements whose probative thrust is to answer the defendant’s knowledge question in context. Justice Thomas’s invocation of DiDomenico and Morales shows a durable circuit practice tolerating modus-operandi generalizations, but precedent-like inertia in the lower courts cannot displace the Rule’s text; at most it suggests courts have been channeling the issue into Rules 702/403 rather than giving 704(b) independent force. Justice Alito is right that Sandstrom is doctrinally distinct, yet the due-process intuition reinforces the textual point: 704(b) is an allocation-of-decisionmaker rule, and it is violated when expert authority functionally supplies the decisive inference on mens rea even if phrased in classwide terms. I therefore maintain that a narrow, context-sensitive “functional equivalent” inquiry is required by the text, with 702/403 as additional (not substitutive) backstops.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability concern is substantial, but his proposed “explicit mens rea opinion only” line creates an easy drafting loophole: as Justice Barrett notes, “about whether” in ordinary usage reaches testimony whose probative thrust is to answer the mens rea question, even if phrased in classwide terms. Justice Gorsuch’s worry that a functional-equivalent approach would swallow Rule 704(a) is overstated under a pragmatic, procedure-protective reading: 704(b) is an express carveout, and courts can still admit neutral trafficking “background” while excluding near-categorical generalizations offered to prove the disputed mental state. Justice Thomas’s reliance on DiDomenico and Morales shows a longstanding circuit safe harbor, but it does not resolve the fairness problem; channeling this into 702/403 alone risks inconsistent protection of the jury’s role, which Congress specifically targeted in 704(b). Sandstrom is not doctrinally controlling, as Roberts and Alito emphasize, yet Sotomayor’s point about the practical, quasi-presumptive effect of authoritative expert testimony reinforces reading 704(b) to cover functional equivalents in this narrow posture.

John Roberts.reasoning: Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b) bars an expert from stating an opinion about whether “the defendant did or did not have a mental state or condition that constitutes an element of the crime charged,” but it does not categorically preclude general “framework” testimony describing how drug-trafficking organizations typically operate when that testimony stops short of saying “this defendant knew.” The challenged testimony here was cast in general terms about organizational practices and left the ultimate inference about Diaz’s knowledge to the jury, fitting within the narrow reading of 704(b) that preserves common modus-operandi evidence while policing direct mens rea opinions. A broader rule—treating any generalization that makes a knowledge inference more likely as barred—would create serious line-drawing problems and unsettle trial practice without clear textual warrant, undermining institutional stability. Any residual risk of undue prejudice is better managed through Rule 403 balancing and limiting instructions rather than an expanded 704(b) prohibition.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Rule 704(b) by its text bars an expert from stating an opinion “about whether the defendant did or did not have a mental state or condition that constitutes an element of the crime charged,” but it does not forbid testimony describing general practices of criminal enterprises that may incidentally support an inference about knowledge. Consistent with early circuit interpretations, courts have drawn the line at whether the expert expressly states the ultimate inference about the defendant’s mens rea; “framework/modus operandi” testimony remains admissible so long as the jury draws the final conclusion. See Fed. R. Evid. 704(b); United States v. DiDomenico, 985 F.2d 1159, 1165 (2d Cir. 1993) (Friendly, J.) (Rule 704(b) forbids expressly stating the inference), and United States v. Morales, 108 F.3d 1031, 1038 (9th Cir. 1997) (en banc) (same). Sandstrom v. Montana, 442 U.S. 510 (1979), concerns mandatory presumptions imposed by law, not the admission of permissive, contextual evidence that leaves the mens rea determination to the jury.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b) bars an expert from stating “an opinion about whether the defendant did or did not have a mental state or condition that constitutes an element of the crime,” but its text does not forbid generalized, modus-operandi testimony about how drug-trafficking organizations typically operate, so long as the expert does not explicitly opine that the defendant knew. Here the agent’s testimony that traffickers generally do not entrust large shipments to unwitting couriers described common practices and left the ultimate inference about Diaz’s knowledge to the jury, fitting within the narrow, textual limitation of 704(b). Practical consequences also counsel against petitioner’s broader reading, which would destabilize the admissibility of routine “framework” evidence needed to help jurors understand unfamiliar criminal methods and would invite unworkable line-drawing over indirect implications. Sandstrom v. Montana addresses unconstitutional mandatory presumptions in jury instructions, not the admissibility of contextual expert evidence, and does not justify expanding 704(b) beyond its terms.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b) bars expert testimony that effectively supplies the jury with the answer to the defendant’s mens rea, and testimony that drug-trafficking organizations “generally do not use unwitting couriers” for large shipments is, in context, the functional equivalent of saying the defendant knew. Even if framed as “modus operandi,” it invites the jury to treat a probabilistic generalization as near-dispositive proof of knowledge, risking an impermissible shortcut on the central disputed element and undermining the jury’s independent role. That danger is especially acute in cases involving vulnerable defendants where access-to-justice concerns counsel against allowing law-enforcement expertise to become a de facto presumption of guilt. Consistent with the constitutional caution reflected in Sandstrom v. Montana against burden-shifting or presumptive reasoning on mental state, I would hold this testimony violates Rule 704(b) when it is used to imply the defendant’s knowledge rather than to explain genuinely complex background issues.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Rule 704(b) bars an expert in a criminal case from stating an opinion “about whether the defendant did or did not have a mental state or condition that constitutes an element of the crime charged.” Testimony that drug-trafficking organizations “generally do not use unwitting couriers for large shipments,” when offered to prove the defendant’s knowledge is the disputed element, functions as an opinion on that element in all but name and risks letting an expert supply what the Rule reserves to the jury. A workable, text-faithful line is that generalized “framework” testimony is permissible only when it explains methods without asserting (directly or effectively) that defendants in the charged posture typically possess the requisite mens rea. That reading also avoids the due-process concern—recognized in cases like Sandstrom v. Montana, 442 U.S. 510 (1979)—that evidentiary devices not become de facto presumptions on a defendant’s mental state.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Rule 704(b)’s text bars an expert from stating an opinion about whether “the defendant did or did not have a mental state” that is an element of the crime, but it does not prohibit experience-based testimony describing general practices of drug-trafficking organizations so long as the expert does not opine on the defendant’s own knowledge. Reading 704(b) to reach any testimony that might support an inference about mens rea would effectively repeal Rule 704(a)’s instruction that opinions are “not automatically objectionable” merely because they embrace an ultimate issue, and it would invite uncertain line-drawing untethered from the Rule’s words. Any remaining concerns about undue prejudice or reliability are addressed, in the first instance, through Rules 702 and 403 rather than by expanding 704(b) beyond its plain meaning, and constitutional mandatory-presumption problems like Sandstrom v. Montana are not presented where the testimony leaves the ultimate inference to the jury. Because the expert here spoke in generalities and did not state that Diaz herself knew, the district court did not violate Rule 704(b).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b) bars an expert from stating an opinion about whether the defendant “did or did not have a mental state” that constitutes an element of the crime, but it does not categorically prohibit expert “framework” testimony describing common practices of drug-trafficking organizations so long as the expert does not expressly opine that the defendant knew about the drugs. Consistent with judicial restraint and the traditional discretion afforded trial courts over evidentiary rulings, admitting general modus operandi testimony is workable and preserves the jury’s role in drawing the ultimate inference about Diaz’s knowledge. While Sandstrom v. Montana cautions against mandatory or burden-shifting presumptions on mens rea, this testimony—properly limited and coupled with instructions—does not compel a finding of knowledge and therefore does not create a Sandstrom-type constitutional problem. Given the text of Rule 704(b) and the practical need for contextual evidence in unfamiliar criminal schemes, I would affirm the Ninth Circuit’s narrower reading that focuses on explicit opinions about the defendant’s mental state.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Rule 704(b) bars an expert from stating an opinion “about whether the defendant did or did not have” the mental state constituting an element of the offense, and the ordinary public meaning of “about whether” reaches testimony that effectively answers the mens rea question even if framed in generalities. A law-enforcement expert’s assertion that drug-trafficking organizations generally do not use unwitting couriers for large shipments functions as classwide mens rea proof—inviting the jury to treat the generalization as an expert endorsement that this defendant knew—thereby crossing the line from permissible modus operandi context to an impermissible opinion on knowledge. That reading also preserves Rule 704(b)’s purpose of keeping the mens rea determination with the jury and avoids turning probabilistic generalizations into a de facto presumption, a concern reflected in Sandstrom v. Montana’s warning against burden-shifting or conclusive inferences on mental state. While background testimony about trafficking methods may be admissible, testimony keyed to whether couriers “know” in “most circumstances” is “about whether” the defendant had the requisite mental state and should have been excluded under Rule 704(b).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Federal Rule of Evidence 704(b) bars expert testimony that states an opinion about whether the defendant had the mental state constituting an element of the crime, and that protection is undermined if the government may introduce the functional equivalent of a mens rea opinion through “general” modus-operandi assertions that large shipments are not entrusted to unwitting couriers. In a case where knowledge is the central disputed element, testimony framed as “D.T.O.s generally don’t use unknowing couriers” invites the jury to treat a probabilistic generalization as a near-presumption of the defendant’s knowledge, raising serious procedural-fairness concerns and risks akin to the impermissible burden-shifting logic cautioned against in Sandstrom v. Montana. While background testimony about trafficking practices can be admissible, Rule 704(b) requires a meaningful line that prevents experts from effectively telling the jury how to decide the defendant’s mental state; the Fifth Circuit’s “functional equivalent” approach better preserves the Rule’s purpose than an “explicit opinion only” standard. Given the practical consequences for criminal trials—especially for defendants asserting lack of knowledge—this testimony should have been excluded or more tightly limited under Rule 704(b).
